Random Variables, Expectation and Jensen's Inequality

A day's return as a random variable: its distribution, its expectation and moments, the tail bounds that need no model, and the inequality that is the real reason for volatility drag.

Volume III · ProbabilityBuilds on LM1 · LM3 · LM4 · LM5 · LM13Leads to LM15 · LM16 · LM17 · LM18 · LM19 · LM20 · LM21 · LM22 · LM26 · LM32 · LM41Time ≈ 2.5 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1describe a discrete or continuous random variable by its pmf or density and its distribution function, and find its quantiles and medians, including those of a sample's empirical distribution
2calculate expectations as probability-weighted sums or integrals, check that they exist, and apply LOTUS and linearity, including to g(f)=E[ln(1+fR)]
3derive E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​, Var(ηX+ζ)=η2Var(X), E[Z4]=3 and Var(Z2)=2, and compute the skewness and kurtosis of a distribution
4apply Markov's, Chebyshev's and Cantelli's inequalities under their conditions, and compare their bounds with TAIEX's tail frequencies
5prove Jensen's inequality and its strict form from the tangent-line property, and derive the weighted AM–GM inequality from it
6explain volatility drag through the Jensen gap ln(1+μ)−g of the logarithm, compute both exactly, and judge when σ2/2 describes them
7compute the distribution, quantiles, moments and tail frequencies of an empirical distribution in Python, stating the quantile and moment conventions
Learning Module Overview
  • A random variable is a function on a sample space. One distribution function FX​(x)=Pr(X≤x) serves discrete and continuous laws, and the quantile function FX−1​(u)=min{x:FX​(x)≥u} always exists, even where FX​(x)=1/2 has no solution.
  • As an empirical distribution, TAIEX's 5,849 daily total returns have a median of 0.0879%, above their mean of 0.0625%, and a longer lower tail: the 0.1% quantile is −6.313%, the 99.9% quantile 5.823%.
  • An expectation is a probability-weighted sum or integral that exists only when it converges absolutely. LOTUS computes E[h(X)] without the law of h(X), and the growth function g(f)=E[ln(1+fR)] is one such expectation.
  • The identity E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​ is the population form of the sample identity (3.7). TAIEX's skewness is −0.34 and its kurtosis 8.27, an excess of 5.27; its fourth moment is 2.72 times that of the normal with the same mean and variance.
  • Markov's, Chebyshev's and Cantelli's inequalities bound tail probabilities with a mean or a variance alone. They hold exactly for TAIEX's empirical law and are loose: 17 days lie at least four standard deviations below the mean, against Cantelli's bound of 344.1.
  • Jensen's inequality, E[h(X)]≤h(EX) for a concave h, follows from one tangent line. It gives the weighted AM–GM inequality and RG​≤μ: the compound rate never exceeds the average return.
  • The Jensen gap ln(1+μ)−g=ln(1+μ)−ln(1+RG​) is volatility drag measured in log points. For TAIEX it is 0.7316 bp a day (the drag μ−RG​ is 0.7320 bp), of which the second-order term gives 0.7292 bp; for annual returns the higher-order terms matter, and for a lognormal law the gap is exactly half the variance of the log return.

1Introduction

LM13 defined a random variable as a function on a sample space. This module computes with random variables. Its central result, Jensen's inequality, compares the average of a function with the function of the average. For the logarithm, the gap between the two is the Jensen gap, LM3's volatility drag measured in log points.

Motivating CaseTwo averages, one market

The TAIEX total-return index reinvests cash dividends. Over the 23 calendar years 2003–2025 (2003 from its first close, 2 January 2003), it returned 14.97% a year on average. An investor who held it throughout earned 12.35% a year. The average of 2008's −43.07% and 2009's +83.34% is +20.1% a year, yet together the two years returned only +4.4%.

Day by day, through 8 October 2026, the average return was 0.0625%, while the compound daily rate was 0.0552%. Their gap, the volatility drag of LM3, is 0.7320 bp, within 0.002 bp of half the daily variance, 0.7301 bp. Why is the compound rate never above the average? What exactly is the drag? And when does σ2/2 describe it?

Sections 2 to 4 cover distributions, expectations and moments, and Section 5 tail bounds. Section 6 proves Jensen's inequality, Section 7 resolves the case, and Section 8 works in Python.

NoteNotation for this module

TAIEX is the total-return index, with daily simple return R and log return r=ln(1+R): T=5,849 returns (a count) from 3 January 2003 to 8 October 2026; the closes from 2 January 2003 span 23.7645 years, so A=246.12. Calendar years are 2003–2025, 2003 from its first close.

  • F^, F^−1, EF^​: the empirical distribution of a sample, its quantile function and its expectation. μ, σ, g=E[ln(1+R)] and the compound rate RG​:=eg−1 belong to R; under F^ they are Rˉ, s, rˉ (divisor T) and LM3's geometric mean return RG​. sr​: the standard deviation of r.
  • Local: xj​, J: the values of a discrete X and their number (J may be infinite), or in Section 6 the numbers of the AM–GM inequality, with weights wj​; R(j)​: the return of rank j from the smallest; h: a generic function on an open interval I (LM4's I is now the identity matrix). Indices: j for values and ranks, t for dates.
  • The volatility drag μ−RG​ and the Jensen gap ln(1+μ)−g have no symbol.
NoteResearch hygiene

Every TAIEX frequency, quantile and moment here describes the sample through its empirical distribution: these numbers are descriptive, not forecasts. The normal model with the same mean and variance is in-sample. The coins, dice, two-point bets and the lognormal form are models, and the lab's comparison of the two price-limit regimes is a stability check. LM17 asks when averages approach expectations, and LM20 treats estimation.

2Random Variables and Their Distributions

describe a discrete or continuous random variable by its pmf or density and its distribution function, and find its quantiles and medians, including those of a sample's empirical distribution

A random variable assigns a number to every outcome of a sample space Ω (LM13). Several outcomes can share a value, and the distribution of X, also called its law, collects their probabilities.

Example 1Two trades as one random variable

LM4's bet returns +2% or −1% with equal probability; at its Kelly exposure f=25, one trade multiplies wealth by 1.5 or 0.75. Two independent trades give LM13's sample space Ω={++,+−,−+,−−}, each outcome with probability ¼. LM13 tabulated the distribution of X=W2​/W0​. Find its distribution function, its 10% quantile and its median.

Solution

The outcomes map to 2.25, 1.125, 1.125 and 0.5625 (Exhibit 2), so pX​(1.125)=21​ and pX​(0.5625)=pX​(2.25)=41​.

The distribution function jumps from ¼ to ¾ at 1.125, so FX​(x)=21​ has no solution. Yet 1.125 is the only median under the definition below, since Pr(X≤1.125)=Pr(X≥1.125)=43​. The 10% quantile, the smallest x with FX​(x)≥0.1, is 0.5625.

Distribution functions and quantiles

A discrete random variable has a probability mass function (pmf) pX​(xj​):=Pr(X=xj​) on its finitely or countably many values xj​ (LM13). A continuous one has a density fX​ (LM5).

DefinitionDistribution function, quantile function and median

The distribution function of a random variable X is FX​(x):=Pr(X≤x), (13.11). For a discrete X it is the sum of pX​(xj​) over all xj​≤x; for a continuous one, the area under fX​ to the left of x. For 0<u<1, the quantile function is

FX−1​(u):=min{x:FX​(x)≥u}.
A value x is a median of X if Pr(X≤x)≥21​ and Pr(X≥x)≥21​.

The minimum exists because FX​ rises from 0 to 1, never decreases and takes the upper value at a jump. When FX​ is continuous and strictly increasing, FX−1​ is its inverse and a median solves FX​(x)=21​, as in LM5. In general the medians form a closed interval, possibly a single point.

A sample as a random variable

A sample becomes a random variable through its empirical distribution F^, (13.12), with mass 1/T on each of TAIEX's T returns, so every frequency is a probability. From this volume on, population names a property of a random variable or a model (μ, σ), and sample a statistic of data (Rˉ, s, divisor T). LM3's "population variance" s2 is the variance of F^.

Quantiles of F^ are order statistics. Sort the returns, which are all distinct, as R(1)​<R(2)​<⋯<R(T)​. Because F^(R(j)​)=j/T, the smallest order statistic with j/T≥u is

F^−1(u)=R(⌈uT⌉)​.

Example 2TAIEX's daily return as a random variable

Treat TAIEX's daily returns as a random variable R under F^. Find F^(0), the median and the 1% and 99% quantiles.

Solution

No day returned exactly 0, and 2,644 days fell, so F^(0)=2,644/5,849=0.4520, the value of LM13; the other 3,205 days (54.8%) rose. Because T is odd, the median is the 2,925th return, 0.0879%, above the mean of 0.0625%: 3,020 days (51.6%) beat the mean.

The lower tail reaches further (Exhibit 3). The 1% quantile is F^−1(0.01)=−3.567%, against F^−1(0.99)=3.125%; at 0.1% it is −6.313%, against 5.823% at 99.9%.

LM32 turns lower quantiles into value at risk; LM15 compares them with a normal model's.

PitfallA median need not solve FX​(x)=21​

A fair coin paying 0 or 1 has FX​(x)=21​ on all of [0,1), and every x in [0,1] is a median. Example 1 has one median, although FX​(x)=21​ has no solution. Software reports one point by its own rule (Section 8), so state the definition.

Knowledge Check 1

A fair die shows 1 to 6, each with probability 1/6. Which values are medians, and what is FX−1​(21​)?

Answer

Every x in [3,4] is a median, since then Pr(X≤x)≥63​ and Pr(X≥x)≥63​. The quantile function picks the smallest, FX−1​(21​)=3, while np.median of the six faces returns the midpoint 3.5.

3Expectation and LOTUS

calculate expectations as probability-weighted sums or integrals, check that they exist, and apply LOTUS and linearity, including to g(f)=E[ln(1+fR)]

An expectation is a probability-weighted average of values.

DefinitionExpectation

Let X take the values xj​, j=1,…,J (J finite or infinite), with pmf pX​. If ∑j​∣xj​∣pX​(xj​)<∞, the expectation E[X] is the sum below; otherwise it does not exist. The indicator 1A​ of an event A is 1 on A and 0 elsewhere, so

E[X]:=j∑​xj​pX​(xj​),E[1A​]=Pr(A).​(14.1)

For a density, LM5's (5.9) is the continuous form, with the same condition. Random variables that are neither discrete nor continuous need a more general integral, which this book does not use. Under F^, (14.1) gives EF^​[R]=Rˉ.

An expectation can fail to exist: LM5's Cauchy density has no mean, and Problem 3 has a discrete case. Why the average of many independent draws approaches the expectation is the law of large numbers of LM17.

TheoremLaw of the unconscious statistician (LOTUS)

Let X be discrete with values xj​, and let h be a function with ∑j​∣h(xj​)∣pX​(xj​)<∞. Then

E[h(X)]=j∑​h(xj​)pX​(xj​).(14.2)

LOTUS weights each value of X by its probability and never needs the pmf of h(X). For densities, (5.9) is LOTUS: when Y=h(X) has a density, (5.9) equals ∫yfY​(y)dy, for a continuous h and an integral that exists. This is stated without proof (Grinstead and Snell 1997, §6.3, Theorem 6.11).

Deep DiveLOTUS by groupingoptional · click to expand

Here yi​, i=1,2,…, are the distinct values of Y=h(X). Countable additivity (LM13) gives Pr(Y=yi​)=∑j:h(xj​)=yi​​pX​(xj​). Grouping the terms of (14.2) by the value of h,

​j∑​h(xj​)pX​(xj​)=i∑​j:h(xj​)=yi​∑​yi​pX​(xj​)=i∑​yi​Pr(Y=yi​),​
which is E[Y] by (14.1). Regrouping a series is allowed when it converges absolutely, the condition of (14.2), and the same regrouping of the absolute values shows that E[Y] exists. ■

PropositionLinearity

Let X and Y be random variables on one sample space whose expectations exist, and let η and ζ be constants. Then

E[ηX+ζ]=ηE[X]+ζ,E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y].​(14.3)

On a countable Ω, grouping the outcomes by the value of X gives E[X]=∑ω​X(ω)Pr(ω), and both identities follow by splitting one absolutely convergent sum into two. For densities, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] is stated without proof (Grinstead and Snell 1997, §6.3, Theorem 6.10). It follows that E[X]≤E[Y] when X≤Y with probability one, since outcomes of probability zero add nothing to the sums.

Example 3Expectation two ways

For the X of Example 1, compute E[X] over the outcomes and over the values. Then compare E[21​lnX], by LOTUS, with 21​lnE[X].

Solution

Over the outcomes, 41​(2.25+1.125+1.125+0.5625)=1.265625, and over the values 41​×0.5625+21​×1.125+41​×2.25=1.265625. That is 1.1252, the product of the two trades' expected factors 1+25×0.5%. The expectation of a product of independent factors is the product of the expectations, a rule that LM16 proves. Here the four outcomes give it directly.

LOTUS with h(x)=21​lnx, the log growth per trade, uses Exhibit 2's last column:

​41​(40.5465%)+21​(5.8892%)+41​(−28.7682%)=5.889%.​
This average is 21​ln1.125, LM4's g∗ again. Against it, 21​lnE[X]=ln1.125=11.778%: here the log of the average is twice the average of the logs.

Example 4The growth function as an expectation

Show that LM4's growth function g(f)=E[ln(1+fR)], (4.1), is LOTUS, and evaluate it for TAIEX at f=1.

Solution

With h(x)=ln(1+fx) and R∈{b,−a}, (14.2) gives (4.7), pln(1+fb)+qln(1−fa). Under F^ it gives (4.4), gˉ​(f)=EF^​[ln(1+fR)].

At f=1, gˉ​(1)=rˉ=5.5170 bp a day. Times A, this is 13.58% a year, which equals ln(25.2007)/23.7645 by (1.12): the log growth over the whole sample, 2026 included. The compound rate is 25.20071/23.7645−1=14.54%.

Differentiating under the expectation, as (4.5) does term by term, needs a condition when R takes infinitely many values; LM41 states it.

PitfallThe expectation of a function is not the function of the expectation

For TAIEX, g=rˉ is not ln(1+Rˉ), which is larger by 0.7316 bp a day (Section 7), and Example 3 shows a factor of two. By (14.3) the two agree for every X when h(x)=ηx+ζ; two-point laws show that no other h does so.

導讀隨機變數、分位數與期望值

隨機變數（random variable）是樣本空間（sample space）上的函數：離散時用機率質量函數（probability mass function），連續時用密度（density），兩者共用同一個累積分布函數（distribution function）FX​(x)=Pr(X≤x)。分位數函數（quantile function）取「使 FX​(x)≥u 的最小 x」，所以一定存在；中位數（median）卻可能是一整段區間，也可能根本解不出 FX​(x)=21​。把加權股價報酬指數 5,849 個日報酬各給 1/T 的機率，就得到經驗分布（empirical distribution），樣本的頻率就是這個模型的機率。樣本平均數（sample mean）就是經驗分布的期望值（expectation）；LM3 所說的母體變異數（population variance）s2，也就是經驗分布的變異數。LOTUS 讓我們不必先求 h(X) 的分布（distribution），直接用 X 的機率加權 h(x)，但函數的期望值一般不等於期望值的函數，g=E[ln(1+R)] 並不等於 ln(1+μ)。

Knowledge Check 2

A day returns +10% or −10% with equal probability. Compute E[R] and E[ln(1+R)].

Answer

The mean return is 0, but E[ln(1+R)]=21​ln1.1+21​ln0.9=21​ln0.99=−0.5025%. The log of the average, ln1=0, is not the average of the logs.

4Variance and Higher Moments

derive E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​, Var(ηX+ζ)=η2Var(X), E[Z4]=3 and Var(Z2)=2, and compute the skewness and kurtosis of a distribution

The variance of X is Var(X):=E[(X−μX​)2], where μX​=E[X], and σX​:=Var(X)​ is its standard deviation.

PropositionSecond moment and variance

If E[X2]<∞, then E[X] exists, and for constants η and ζ

E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​,Var(ηX+ζ)=η2Var(X).​(14.4)

The mean exists because ∣x∣≤1+x2 for every x. Expanding the square with (14.3) gives E[(X−μX​)2]=E[X2]−2μX​E[X]+μX2​=E[X2]−μX2​. For the second identity, ηX+ζ has mean ημX​+ζ, so its deviation from the mean is η(X−μX​).

Under F^, (14.4) is LM3's identity (3.7), T1​∑t​Rt2​=s2+Rˉ2; in a model it is LM4's E[R2]=σ2+μ2. The variance of a sum needs the covariance of its terms (LM16). By (14.4), (X−μX​)/σX​ has mean 0 and variance 1, as LM5's (5.5) used for the normal. Since x2≤1+x4 and ∣x∣3≤1+x4, a finite fourth moment makes every lower moment finite.

DefinitionSkewness and kurtosis

Let E[X4]<∞ and σX​>0. The skewness and the kurtosis of X are its third and fourth standardized moments,

Skew(X):=σX3​E[(X−μX​)3]​,Kurt(X):=σX4​E[(X−μX​)4]​,​(14.5)
and the excess kurtosis is Kurt(X)−3. The skewness needs only E∣X∣3<∞.

Both are unchanged when X becomes ηX+ζ with η>0, because the deviation and σX​ scale by the same η. Applied to a sample, (14.5) gives the sample skewness and kurtosis. The choice of T or T−1, and how far such numbers move between samples, are questions for LM19 and LM20.

Example 5Moments of the +2%/−1% bet

Compute the moments of LM4's bet, +2% or −1% with equal probability, up to the kurtosis.

Solution

The mean is μ=0.5%, and the deviations are ±1.5%, so σ=1.5% and E[R2]=21​(0.022+0.012)=0.00025=σ2+μ2. The raw third moment is 21​(0.023−0.013)=3.5×10−6, which equals μ3+3μσ2, as in LM4's Practice Problem 13.

The deviations are symmetric, so the skewness is 0, although the raw third moment is positive. Every squared deviation equals σ2, so the kurtosis is 1, an excess kurtosis of −2.

The normal's moments

For a standard normal Z the odd moments vanish by symmetry, and E[Z2]=1 (LM5). Integration by parts, (5.6), moves one factor z onto φ, since zφ(z) is the derivative of −φ(z):

E[Z4]​=∫−∞∞​z3⋅zφ(z)dz=[−z3φ(z)]−∞∞​+3E[Z2]=3.​
Hence Var(Z2)=E[Z4]−(E[Z2])2=2, the value LM3 used without proof. For a normal X=μ+σZ, expanding the powers of μ+σZ and dropping the odd moments of Z gives
E[Z3]=0,E[Z4]=3,Var(Z2)=2,E[X3]=μ3+3μσ2,E[X4]=μ4+6μ2σ2+3σ4.​(14.6)
So the normal has skewness 0 and kurtosis 3, which LM5 stated without proof. Excess kurtosis measures tail weight against this benchmark.

Example 6TAIEX against the normal

Compare TAIEX's moments under F^ with those of N(Rˉ,s2). Then size the terms that LM4's normal approximations E[R3]≈3μσ2 and E[R4]≈3σ4 drop.

Solution

Under F^, (14.5) gives a skewness of −0.34 and a kurtosis of 8.27, an excess kurtosis of 5.27 (Exhibit 4). The raw third moment is −3.231×10−7, against the normal's +2.740×10−7 from (14.6). The fourth moment, 1.751×10−7, is 2.72 times the normal's 6.430×10−8; LM4 found 3.7 for 0050, another sample. LM15 fits distributions to TAIEX; this normal is only a benchmark.

By (14.6), the approximations drop terms of relative size (Rˉ/s)2=0.0027: a share 31​(Rˉ/s)2=0.09% of 3Rˉs2=2.738×10−7, and a share 2(Rˉ/s)2+31​(Rˉ/s)4=0.54% of 3s4=6.396×10−8.

PitfallA raw third moment is not skewness, and kurtosis is not excess kurtosis

Expanding E[(μ+(R−μ))3] gives E[R3]=μ3+3μσ2+E[(R−μ)3]: the raw moment mixes the mean into the asymmetry, so Example 5's bet has E[R3]>0 and zero skewness. Kurtosis and excess kurtosis differ by 3: TAIEX's 8.27 is 5.27 in excess, the number to set beside 0050's 8.12. Say "excess" whenever such a number meets LM4, LM5 or LM15.

導讀動差：分布形狀的摘要

動差（moment）是 X 各次方的期望值（expectation）；變異數（variance）是二階中心動差（central moment），而 E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​ 正是 LM3 恆等式 (3.7) 的母體（population）版本。把 X 減去平均數（mean）、除以標準差（standard deviation）以後再取三次方與四次方的期望值，就是標準化動差（standardized moment），分別稱為偏態（skewness）與峰態（kurtosis）。常態分布（normal distribution）的峰態是 3，所以峰態減 3 叫超額峰態（excess kurtosis）。加權股價報酬指數日報酬的偏態是 −0.34、峰態 8.27，四階動差是同平均數、同變異數常態的 2.72 倍，大波動比常態多。原始三階動差（raw third moment）不是偏態，因為它混入了平均數：+2%/−1% 賭局的三階動差為正，偏態卻是 0。

Knowledge Check 3

A fund returns 2R, twice TAIEX's daily return. What are its standard deviation and E[(2R)2], and do its skewness and kurtosis change?

Answer

By (14.4) the standard deviation doubles, 2s=2.417%; four decimals would need s to five, since 2×1.2084=2.4168 while 2s=2.41673%. The second moment quadruples, 4E[R2]=5.856×10−4. Skewness and kurtosis do not change, because η=2>0.

5Tail Bounds: Markov, Chebyshev and Cantelli

apply Markov's, Chebyshev's and Cantelli's inequalities under their conditions, and compare their bounds with TAIEX's tail frequencies

How often can a random variable stray far from its mean, if only its mean or its variance is known? Three inequalities answer without a model.

TheoremMarkov's inequality

If X≥0 with probability one and x>0, then

Pr(X≥x)≤xE[X]​.(14.7)

Proof. With probability one, x1{X≥x}≤X: the left side is x when X≥x and 0 otherwise. Taking expectations with (14.1) and monotonicity gives xPr(X≥x)≤E[X]. ■

TheoremChebyshev's and Cantelli's inequalities

Let X have a finite variance with σX​>0. For k>0,

Pr(∣X−μX​∣≥kσX​)≤k21​,(14.8)
and for k≥0 the lower tail alone satisfies
Pr(X−μX​≤−kσX​)≤1+k21​.(14.9)

Chebyshev's (14.8) is Markov's inequality for (X−μX​)2 at the level k2σX2​, since E[(X−μX​)2]=σX2​. Cantelli's one-sided (14.9) needs a shift (Deep Dive below). Simple laws attain both bounds, so neither can be improved for every law.

For k≤1 Chebyshev's bound says nothing. Without a finite variance, as for the Pareto law of Problem 7, neither bound applies. Under F^, with μ=Rˉ and σ=s (divisor T), every bound holds exactly, because F^ is a probability law with these moments.

Deep DiveCantelli's inequality, and the laws that attain the boundsoptional · click to expand

Here t>0 is a shift, not a date. If X−μX​≤−kσX​, then μX​−X+t≥kσX​+t>0, so

{X−μX​≤−kσX​}⊆{(μX​−X+t)2≥(kσX​+t)2}.​
The variable μX​−X+t has mean t and variance σX2​, so its square has expectation σX2​+t2 by (14.4). Markov's (14.7) then gives
Pr(X−μX​≤−kσX​)≤(kσX​+t)2σX2​+t2​.
For k>0 the derivative in t vanishes where tkσX​=σX2​, so the bound is smallest at t=σX​/k, where it equals 1/(1+k2). At k=0 the bound 1 is trivial.

The law with μX​−kσX​ with probability 1/(1+k2) and μX​+σX​/k otherwise has mean μX​ and variance σX2​, and it attains (14.9). For k≥1, the law with μX​±kσX​ with probability 1/(2k2) each and μX​ otherwise attains (14.8). ■

Example 7Three bounds for a 3% day

Bound the share of TAIEX days with ∣R∣≥3% by Markov's inequality on ∣R∣ and on R2, and the share with R≤−3% by Cantelli's. Use E∣R∣=0.8402%, E[R2]=1.464×10−4, Rˉ=0.0625% and s=1.2084%.

Solution

Markov's inequality on ∣R∣ gives Pr(∣R∣≥3%)≤0.8402/3=28.0%. On R2 the event is {R2≥0.032}, with the bound 1.464×10−4/0.0009=16.27%, tighter because R2 weights large moves more. The data have 175 such days, 2.99%.

For the lower tail, −3%=Rˉ−ks with k=(0.0625+3)/1.2084=2.534. Cantelli's bound is 1/(1+2.5342)=13.47%; the data have 108 days at or below −3% (LM13), 1.85%.

Example 8Four standard deviations below the mean

LM5's Practice Problem 9 set a normal four-sigma probability beside Cantelli's bound. Repeat it on TAIEX: how many days fell at least four standard deviations below the mean?

Solution

The threshold is Rˉ−4s=−4.771%. Cantelli's bound is 1/17=5.88% of the days, and the normal model gives Φ(−4)=3.17×10−5, or 0.185 expected days in 5,849. TAIEX had 17 such days (0.29%): 92 times the normal's expected count and about a twentieth of the bound. These ratios are descriptive, not a test.

Two-sided, 30 days (0.51%) moved at least four standard deviations either way (Exhibit 6). Chebyshev's bound is 6.25%, and the normal model expects 0.37 days.

PitfallA bound is not a model

The bounds hold for every law with the given variance, even the simple laws that attain them. So they lie far above real frequencies: 17 days against 344.1 at k=4 (Exhibit 5). Read neither a bound nor the normal's 0.185 days as an estimate of risk; LM15 fits models to the tails.

導讀只知道平均數與變異數時

馬可夫不等式（Markov's inequality）只用到 X≥0 與平均數（mean）：門檻乘上指示函數（indicator）永遠不超過 X 本身，取期望值（expectation）就得到上界（bound）。對 (X−μX​)2 用同一招，就是謝比雪夫不等式（Chebyshev's inequality），上界是 1/k2。加上一個平移再用一次，得到單邊的 Cantelli 不等式（Cantelli's inequality），上界是 1/(1+k2)。這些上界對所有變異數（variance）有限的分布（distribution）都成立，所以對加權股價報酬指數的經驗分布（empirical distribution）也一定成立，但很鬆：低於平均數至少四個標準差（standard deviation）的上界是 344.1 天，實際只有 17 天。上界不是模型，常態模型算出的 0.185 天也不是風險估計；尾部模型留給 LM15。

Knowledge Check 4

What does Chebyshev's inequality say at k=1? At k=2, compare its two-sided bound with Cantelli's one-sided bound and with TAIEX.

Answer

At k=1 the bound is 1, which says nothing. At k=2, Chebyshev allows 25% of the days two standard deviations away on either side, and Cantelli 20% on the lower side alone. TAIEX had 319 days (5.45%) and 188 days (3.21%).

6Jensen's Inequality

prove Jensen's inequality and its strict form from the tangent-line property, and derive the weighted AM–GM inequality from it

For a two-point return the logarithm's concavity is visible: the chord between the two outcomes on the curve ln(1+x) lies below the curve. Above the mean μ, the chord gives the average of the logs, g, and the curve the log of the average, ln(1+μ). The widget starts from 2008 and 2009 with equal probability: μ=20.1%, but g=2.141% against ln(1+μ)=18.345%.

TheoremJensen's inequality

Let h be concave and differentiable on an open interval I, and let X be a random variable with

  • values in I with probability one,
  • finite expectations E∣X∣ and E∣h(X)∣.

Then

E[h(X)]≤h(E[X]).(14.10)
If h is strictly concave, equality holds only when Pr(X=μX​)=1. For a convex h both inequalities reverse.

Proof. The mean μX​ lies in I. Indeed, X lies in the open interval I with probability one, so its distance to a finite end is positive with probability one. By (14.3), this distance has mean μX​ minus a lower end, or an upper end minus μX​, at least 0 by monotonicity. It is not 0: if a variable Y>0 with probability one had mean 0, Markov's (14.7) would give Pr(Y≥x)=0 for every x>0. Countable additivity would then give Pr(Y>0)=0.

By LM4's Deep Dive on tangent lines, the concave h lies below its tangent at μX​: for every x∈I,

h(x)≤h(μX​)+h′(μX​)(x−μX​).
Put x=X, which lies in I with probability one, and take expectations with (14.3) and monotonicity: E[h(X)]≤h(μX​)+h′(μX​)(E[X]−μX​)=h(μX​). ■

The proof needs only the tangent line, which covers every h in this book. For a convex h, apply (14.10) to −h: with h(x)=ex it gives E[eX]≥eEX, and LM5's (5.12) measures the gap for a normal X, E[eX]=eμX​+σX2​/2.

Deep DiveThe strict formoptional · click to expand

Here xmid​ is a midpoint and ε a small positive number. Let h be strictly concave and differentiable on I, and let x=μX​ lie in I, with xmid​:=(x+μX​)/2. Strict concavity puts h(xmid​) strictly above the chord, and the tangent at μX​ lies above h at xmid​:

​21​h(x)+21​h(μX​)<h(xmid​)≤h(μX​)+h′(μX​)2x−μX​​.​
Doubling and subtracting h(μX​) gives the strict tangent inequality h(x)<h(μX​)+h′(μX​)(x−μX​) for every x=μX​.

So the tangent gap h(μX​)+h′(μX​)(X−μX​)−h(X) is non-negative, positive when X=μX​, and has expectation h(μX​)−E[h(X)]. If Pr(X=μX​)>0, countable additivity gives some ε>0 for which the gap is at least ε with positive probability. Markov's (14.7) then makes its expectation at least ε times that probability, so (14.10) is strict. ■

PropositionWeighted AM–GM inequality

Let x1​,…,xJ​>0, and let the weights satisfy wj​≥0 and ∑j​wj​=1. Then

j∑​wj​xj​≥j∏​xjwj​​,(14.11)
with equality if and only if all xj​ with wj​>0 are equal.

Let X take the value xj​ with probability wj​: the weights qualify as probabilities because they are non-negative and sum to 1. The logarithm is strictly concave on I=(0,∞), so (14.10) gives ∑j​wj​lnxj​≤ln∑j​wj​xj​; exponentiate. By the strict form, equality needs equal xj​ wherever wj​>0.

With wj​=1/J this is the strict unweighted inequality that LM1 used for its compounding sequence. With xj​=erj​ and logs, (14.11) is LM1's (1.14) for a long-only portfolio.

Example 9The case's first question

Apply (14.11) to Exhibit 1's 23 calendar-year growth factors with equal weights, and to 2008 and 2009 alone.

Solution

With wj​=1/23, the left side is one plus the arithmetic mean, 1.1497, and the right side one plus the compound rate, 1.1235. The compound rate cannot exceed the average, and with unequal factors it lies strictly below.

For 2008 and 2009 alone, 21​(0.5693+1.8334)=1.20135, while 0.5693×1.8334​=1.02164. The pair's compound rate is 2.16% a year against an average of 20.1%.

PitfallCheck the direction and the weights

Jensen's inequality reverses for a convex h, so check the sign of h′′ first (LM4; Simon and Blume 1994, chapter 21). Its weights must be probabilities. LM1's weights (1.5,−0.5), a short position, are not, and (1.14) fails for them; Problem 8 shows where the proof breaks.

導讀Jensen 不等式：切線的期望值

凹函數（concave function）的圖形在每一條切線（tangent line）的下方。在平均數（mean）μX​ 取切線，代入 X 再取期望值（expectation），切線部分的期望值剛好等於 h(μX​)，於是得到 E[h(X)]≤h(EX)，這就是 Jensen 不等式（Jensen's inequality）；凸函數（convex function）的方向相反。條件要記清楚：X 必須以機率 1 落在 h 的開區間（open interval）內，而且兩個期望值都存在。把權重看成機率、取 h=ln，就得到加權算幾不等式（weighted AM–GM inequality）。權重必須非負且總和為 1，放空造成的負權重不是機率，不等式就可能不成立。

Knowledge Check 5

Apply (14.10) to the convex function h(x)=x2. What inequality results, and what is the difference between its two sides?

Answer

For a convex h the inequality reverses: E[X2]≥(EX)2. By (14.4) the difference is E[X2]−μX2​=Var(X), which is zero only for a constant X.

7Volatility Drag and the Jensen Gap

explain volatility drag through the Jensen gap ln(1+μ)−g of the logarithm, compute both exactly, and judge when σ2/2 describes them

Apply Jensen's inequality to the growth factor 1+R, with the logarithm as h.

ResultThe compound rate never exceeds the mean

Let R>−1 with probability one, with E∣R∣ and E∣ln(1+R)∣ finite. Then

g≤ln(1+μ),soRG​≤μ,(14.12)
with equality if and only if Pr(R=μ)=1.

Under F^, g=rˉ and RG​ is LM3's geometric mean return, so for any returns the compound rate never exceeds the average. The condition R>−1 matters: a normal R puts positive probability below −1, where ln(1+R) is undefined, so E[ln(1+R)] does not exist and SciPy returns nan. LM4's quadratic approximation (4.2) hides this; a lognormal model, with ln(1+R) normal, keeps R>−1.

Two names for the gap

The volatility drag is LM3's μ−RG​ (Rˉ−RG​ in a sample), in percentage points; the Jensen gap is ln(1+μ)−g, in log points. Since 1+RG​=eg,

μ−RG​=(1+μ)(1−e−(ln(1+μ)−g)),
so the drag is about 1+μ times the Jensen gap when both are small.

The Jensen gap has an exact series. Suppose that R takes finitely many values, each with ∣R−μ∣<1+μ, and write

ln(1+R)=ln(1+μ)+ln(1+1+μR−μ​).
LM3's series (3.3) converges at every value of the last term, and taking expectations term by term, with E[R−μ]=0, gives
ln(1+μ)−g​=2(1+μ)2σ2​−3(1+μ)3E[(R−μ)3]​+4(1+μ)4E[(R−μ)4]​−⋯​(14.13)
The third-order term is −Skew⋅σ3/(3(1+μ)3), so negative skewness widens the gap. To second order in the returns, the factor 1/(1+μ)2 is 1 and the gap is σ2/2, the drag of LM3's (3.8) and (3.9).

For a lognormal law the gap needs no series. If ln(1+R) is normal with mean g and standard deviation σr​, LM5's (5.12) gives 1+μ=E[eln(1+R)]=eg+σr2​/2. The Jensen gap is then exactly σr2​/2, half the variance of the log return rather than of R.

Example 10The Jensen gap and the drag, exactly

Compute TAIEX's daily Jensen gap and drag, and split the gap into the terms of (14.13). Repeat for the calendar years and for 2008 and 2009, and compare the lognormal form.

Solution

Daily, ln(1+Rˉ)−rˉ=0.7316 bp. The second-, third- and fourth-order terms of (14.13) are 0.7292+0.0020+0.0004 bp; negative skewness adds the third. The drag is Rˉ−RG​=(1+Rˉ)(1−e−0.7316 bp)=0.7320 bp, against s2/2=0.7301 bp (Exhibit 7).

For the calendar years, the Jensen gap is 2.31 log points, against 2.12 at second order and 2.30 through the fourth; the drag is 2.62 percentage points, against σ2/2=2.81. For 2008 and 2009, the Jensen gap is 16.20, against 13.84 and 15.76, and the drag is 17.97, against 19.97. With moves this large the series converges slowly.

The lognormal form uses TAIEX's sr​=1.2107%: sr2​/2=0.7329 bp, against the Jensen gap of 0.7316 bp.

Within each calendar year of daily returns, half the variance describes the drag almost exactly (Exhibit 8).

Leverage enlarges the gap: applied to fR, (14.12) gives g(f)≤ln(1+fμ), and the second-order term grows like f2 (LM41). Which of the two rates an investor lives through over many periods is the subject of LM17.

Pitfallσ2/2 is a second-order term

At daily frequency σ2/2 misses TAIEX's drag by under 0.002 bp. For the calendar years, (3.9) gives 14.97%−23.70%2/2=12.16% (12.17% from unrounded inputs), against the actual 12.35%; for 2008 and 2009, 0.16% against 2.16%. And (14.13) and (3.9) use the variance of R, the lognormal form that of r (0.7329 against 0.7301 bp).

導讀波動拖累的真正原因

對 1+R 套用 Jensen 不等式（Jensen's inequality），取 h=ln，對數報酬（log return）的期望值（expectation）g 就不超過 ln(1+μ)，所以複利報酬率（compound rate）RG​ 永遠不超過算術平均（arithmetic mean）μ。兩者的差距有兩種量法：波動拖累（volatility drag）μ−RG​ 以百分點計，Jensen 差距（Jensen gap）ln(1+μ)−g 以對數點（log points）計。把對數展開成級數（series），Jensen 差距的二階項是 σ2/(2(1+μ)2)，三階項由偏態（skewness）決定，四階項由峰態（kurtosis）決定，LM3 的 σ2/2 只是二階近似。日報酬時二階項幾乎完全精準，年報酬或 2008、2009 年這種大波動時，高階項就不能忽略。若對數報酬服從常態分布（normal distribution），也就是對數常態分布（lognormal distribution）模型，Jensen 差距恰好等於對數報酬變異數（variance）的一半 σr2​/2。

Knowledge Check 6

A fund doubles TAIEX's daily return. Compare its daily Jensen gap, ln(1+2Rˉ)−EF^​[ln(1+2R)], with four times the gap at f=1.

Answer

The gap is 2.936 bp, against 4×0.7316=2.926 bp. The second-order term grows like f2, and the higher-order terms, which grow faster, add the rest.

8Random Variables and Expectations in Python

compute the distribution, quantiles, moments and tail frequencies of an empirical distribution in Python, stating the quantile and moment conventions

A NumPy array of returns is its empirical distribution, provided each call uses the right convention (Exhibit 9).

Every count against a threshold uses one guard, R <= c + 1e-12 for R≤c and R >= c - 1e-12 for R≥c. Index levels have two decimals, so a round return can be an exact tie that floating-point division puts on either side of the threshold. At −3% the guard and an exact count with fractions both give 108.

Python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# R: TAIEX's 5,849 daily total returns as a NumPy array
Rbar, s = R.mean(), R.std()                     # divisor T
q = np.quantile(R, 0.001, method="inverted_cdf")  # R_(6), -6.313%
z = (R - Rbar) / s
lower4 = int((z <= -4 + 1e-12).sum())          # 17 days, with the guard
excess = stats.kurtosis(R)                      # 5.27, excess kurtosis
gap = np.log1p(Rbar) - np.log1p(R).mean()      # Jensen gap, 0.7316 bp
Pitfallnp.quantile's default interpolates

By default, np.quantile interpolates between order statistics and can return a value that is no day's return. At u=0.001 it gives −5.866%, against F^−1(0.001)=−6.313%: the interpolation pulls a far-tail quantile towards the centre. Pass method="inverted_cdf" for the quantile function, and state the method with every quantile.

In PythonCompanion lab

The Polars-first notebook LM14_lab.ipynb rebuilds the module's exhibits and computational examples, works the computational practice problems, and ends with a stability check across the two price-limit regimes.

The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

Knowledge Check 7

Which call returns F^−1(0.001) for TAIEX, and what does the other call return?

Answer

np.quantile(R, 0.001, method="inverted_cdf") returns R(6)​=−6.313%; the default returns −5.866%, an interpolated value.

Summary

  • A random variable maps outcomes to numbers. One distribution function serves discrete and continuous laws, the quantile function always exists, and the medians form a closed interval.
  • Under its empirical distribution F^, a sample's frequencies are probabilities, F^−1(u)=R(⌈uT⌉)​, and its divisor-T statistics are population moments.
  • Expectation (14.1) needs absolute convergence; LOTUS (14.2) and linearity (14.3) compute it.
  • The identity E[X2]=σX2​+μX2​, (14.4), is (3.7) for any law; a normal has E[Z4]=3, (14.6). TAIEX has skewness −0.34 and excess kurtosis 5.27.
  • The bounds (14.7)–(14.9) hold exactly but loosely: 17 TAIEX days at k=4 against 344.1.
  • Jensen's inequality (14.10) follows from one tangent line and gives (14.11) and RG​≤μ, (14.12).
  • The Jensen gap ln(1+μ)−g has the exact series (14.13). To second order in the returns, its leading term is LM3's σ2/2: accurate for daily returns, not for annual ones. For a lognormal law the gap is σr2​/2.

Practice Problems

  1. Four independent days of LM4's bet at f=1 (+2% or −1%, equal probability) give the growth factor G=1.02j0.994−j after j up days. Its values 0.960596, 0.989705, 1.019696, 1.050596 and 1.082432 have probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16 and 1/16. Which statement is true, with medians as in Section 2?

    • A.Its only median is 1.019696, below its mean 1.020151.
    • B.Every value from 0.989705 to 1.019696 is a median.
    • C.Its median is its mean, 1.020151.

Why do the skewness and the kurtosis not change, and what does an excess kurtosis near TAIEX's say about a two-point law?

  5. Show E[Z6]=15 by integration by parts, and deduce Var(Z3). For an illustrative X∼N(0.05,0.202), compute E[X3] and E[X4] exactly with (14.6), and check them with stats.norm(0.05, 0.2).moment.

  6. With TAIEX's printed Rˉ=0.0625% and s=1.2084% (divisor T), bound the share of days with R≤−5% by Cantelli's and by Chebyshev's inequality. Give k to four decimals and shares to two decimals of a percent. Compare with the 15 such days of LM13. Which bound is tighter, and why must both hold for F^?

  7. For the Pareto variable of Problem 3, what does Chebyshev's inequality say about Pr(∣X−μX​∣≥3σX​)?

    • A.It is at most 11.1%.
    • B.Nothing, because the variance is infinite.
    • C.It is at most 10%.

  8. Prove (14.11) from (14.10), saying where each condition enters. Then take LM1's weights (1.5,−0.5) and log returns (0.10,0.20): show where the proof fails, and compare ln(1.5e0.10−0.5e0.20) with 1.5×0.10−0.5×0.20 to four decimals.

  9. Which inequality holds for every positive X whose expectations below exist? Check each, to four decimals, on Problem 4's trade at its Kelly exposure: X=1+8R is 1.08 with probability 0.9 and 0.60 otherwise.

    • A.The inequality E[lnX]≥lnE[X]
    • B.The inequality E[1/X]≤1/E[X]
    • C.The inequality E[X​]≤E[X]​

  10. TAIEX's calendar-year returns 2003–2025 (2003 from its first close) have μ=14.97%, σ=23.70% (divisor 23), skewness 0.19 and kurtosis 5.02. (a) Approximate the compound rate by (3.9). (b) Compute the three terms of (14.13) through the fourth order, their sum and the implied RG​=(1+μ)e−gap−1. (c) The actual rate is 12.35%: which term matters most, and why? Give rates to two decimals of a percent, terms to four decimals of a log point.

  11. (Python) Use the lab's TAIEX file, with divisor T. Give A to two decimals, rates to four decimals of a percent, quantiles to three, and the Jensen gap and its terms to four decimals of a bp. (a) Compute T, A, Rˉ and s, and check (3.7). (b) Compute F^−1(0.001) as R(⌈uT⌉)​ and with np.quantile's default. (c) Recount Exhibit 6's days at k=2,3,4 with the guard. (d) Compute the daily Jensen gap and the three terms of (14.13).

Solutions

  1. A is correct. The distribution function is 5/16 just below 1.019696 and 11/16 at it, so Pr(G≤1.019696) and Pr(G≥1.019696) are both 11/16; no other value qualifies. The mean is 1.0054=1.020151 (Solution 2). B reads the flat stretch of FG​ as medians, but FG​=5/16 there. C fails because Pr(G≥1.020151)=5/16.

  2. The distribution function is 1/16, 5/16, 11/16, 15/16 and 1 at the five values. By (14.1), the binomial theorem gives E[G]=((1.02+0.99)/2)4=1.0054=1.02015 (LM16 gives the product rule behind it). By linearity, E[lnG]=4×0.487615%=1.95046%, while lnE[G]=4ln1.005=1.99502%. The Jensen gap, 4.456 bp, is positive by (14.10): the logarithm is strictly concave and G is not constant.

  3. C is correct: the mean is ∫1∞​x⋅1.5x−2.5dx=1.5/0.5=3. In A every term 2j⋅2−j equals 1, so the sum diverges. In B the integral of ∣x∣/(1+x2) diverges like a logarithm.

  4. The mean is μ=0.9×1%−0.1×5%=0.4%. The deviations are +0.6% and −5.4%, so σ2=0.9×0.36+0.1×29.16=3.24 (%²) and σ=1.8%. Then E[R2]=3.4×10−4=σ2+μ2 and E[R3]=0.9×10−6−0.1×1.25×10−4=−1.16×10−5.

    The standardized values are +31​ (probability 0.9) and −3, so the skewness is 0.9/27−0.1×27=−8/3=−2.67 and the kurtosis 0.9/81+0.1×81=73/9=8.11, an excess of 5.11. At f=8 the return is 8R, with μ=3.2%, σ=14.4%, E[(8R)2]=64×3.4×10−4=0.02176, which is 0.1442+0.0322, and E[(8R)3]=512×(−1.16×10−5)=−0.0059392. The standardized values do not change, so by (14.5) neither do the skewness and kurtosis.

    The excess kurtosis is close to TAIEX's 5.27, yet this law has no tail: kurtosis measures how much of the variance comes from rare large deviations, here one rare loss. One number cannot tell a fat tail from a rare jump.

  5. Moving one factor z onto φ as in Section 4, E[Z6]=[−z5φ(z)]−∞∞​+5E[Z4]=15, and Var(Z3)=E[Z6]−02=15. With μ=0.05 and σ2=0.04, (14.6) gives E[X3]=0.000125+0.006=0.006125 and E[X4]=0.00000625+0.0006+0.0048=0.00540625, the values SciPy returns.

  6. Here k=(0.0625+5)/1.2084=4.1894, so Cantelli's bound is 1/(1+k2)=5.39%. Chebyshev's two-sided event contains the lower tail, so 1/k2=5.70% bounds it too, less tightly. The data have 15 days, 0.26%. Both hold because F^ is a probability law with mean Rˉ and variance s2.

  7. B is correct. The integral ∫1∞​x2⋅1.5x−2.5dx diverges, so the variance is infinite and (14.8) does not apply. A uses 1/32 without that condition. C is Cantelli's 1/(1+32), which needs a finite variance too and bounds one tail only.

  8. Let X take the value xj​ with probability wj​, which needs non-negative weights summing to 1. Positive xj​ put X in I=(0,∞), where the logarithm is strictly concave and differentiable; finitely many values make both expectations finite. Then (14.10) gives ∑j​wj​lnxj​≤ln∑j​wj​xj​; exponentiate, and use the strict form for equality.

    With weights (1.5,−0.5) one probability would be −0.5, so no such X exists. Indeed, 1.5e0.10−0.5e0.20=1.0471, whose logarithm, 0.0460, lies below 0.0500.

  9. C is correct. The square root is concave, so (14.10) gives E[X​]≤E[X]​: 1.0128 against 1.0159. A reverses (14.10) for the logarithm: E[lnX]=1.82% against lnE[X]=3.15%. B reverses it for the convex 1/x: E[1/X]=1 exceeds 1/E[X]=0.9690. Here E[1/X]=1 exactly, because LM4's Kelly condition E[R/(1+fR)]=0 gives E[1/(1+fR)]=1.

  10. (a) By (3.9), RG​≈14.97%−23.70%2/2=12.16%. (b) The terms are 0.23702/(2×1.14972)=2.1247, −0.19×0.23703/(3×1.14973)=−0.0555 and 5.02×0.23704/(4×1.14974)=0.2266 log points, with sum 2.2958, so RG​=1.1497e−0.022958−1=12.36%.

    (c) The second-order term carries most of the gap, but alone it gives RG​=12.55%. Adding the fourth-order term, large because the kurtosis is 5.02, gives 12.30%. The third-order term is small because the skewness is, and it raises the estimate to 12.36%.

    (3.9) misses for another reason: it subtracts σ2/2=2.81 points as the drag. The drag is about 1+μ times the gap, so its leading term is σ2/(2(1+μ))=2.44 points, and the higher terms bring it to the actual 2.62.

  11. (a) The sample has T=5,849 returns, A=246.12, Rˉ=0.0625% and s=1.2084%; (3.7) reads 1.464×10−4=1.460×10−4+3.907×10−7. (b) The quantile is R(6)​=−6.313%; the default gives −5.866%. (c) Two-sided, 319, 99 and 30 days; lower, 188, 61 and 17. (d) The Jensen gap is 0.7316 bp, with terms 0.7292+0.0020+0.0004 bp.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Random variable 隨機變數 A function that assigns a number to each outcome of a sample space.
Distribution (law) 分布 The probabilities with which a random variable takes its values, given by pX​ or fX​ and by FX​.
Probability mass function 機率質量函數 pX​(xj​)=Pr(X=xj​) for a discrete X.
Distribution function 累積分布函數 FX​(x)=Pr(X≤x), for discrete and continuous X alike.
Quantile function 分位數函數 FX−1​(u)=min{x:FX​(x)≥u}, 0<u<1.
Median 中位數 A value x with Pr(X≤x)≥21​ and Pr(X≥x)≥21​; the medians form a closed interval.
Empirical distribution 經驗分布 F^: mass 1/T on each observation of a sample.
Order statistic 順序統計量 R(j)​, the observation of rank j from the smallest; F^−1(u)=R(⌈uT⌉)​.
Population; sample 母體；樣本 A property of a random variable or model; a statistic of data, with its divisor stated.
Expectation 期望值 E[X]=∑j​xj​pX​(xj​), (14.1), or (5.9) for a density, when it converges absolutely.
Indicator 指示函數 1A​: 1 on the event A, 0 elsewhere; E[1A​]=Pr(A).
LOTUS LOTUS E[h(X)]=∑j​h(xj​)pX​(xj​), (14.2).
Variance 變異數 Var(X)=E[(X−μX​)2]=E[X2]−μX2​, (14.4).
Skewness; kurtosis 偏態；峰態 Third and fourth standardized moments, (14.5).
Excess kurtosis 超額峰態 Kurtosis minus 3, the normal's value.
Markov's inequality 馬可夫不等式 Pr(X≥x)≤E[X]/x for X≥0 and x>0, (14.7).
Chebyshev's inequality 謝比雪夫不等式 Pr(∣X−μX​∣≥kσX​)≤1/k2, (14.8).
Cantelli's inequality Cantelli 不等式 Pr(X−μX​≤−kσX​)≤1/(1+k2), (14.9).
Jensen's inequality Jensen 不等式 E[h(X)]≤h(EX) for a concave h, (14.10); reversed for a convex h.
Weighted AM–GM inequality 加權算幾不等式 ∑j​wj​xj​≥∏j​xjwj​​ for xj​>0, wj​≥0 and ∑j​wj​=1, (14.11).
Compound rate 複利報酬率 RG​=eg−1, the constant rate with the same growth, LM3's geometric mean return (幾何平均報酬); RG​≤μ, (14.12).
Volatility drag 波動拖累 μ−RG​ (Rˉ−RG​ in a sample), in percentage points.
Jensen gap Jensen 差距 ln(1+μ)−g, in log points, with the series (14.13).
